summary_plain: This investigation burned gas fuels such as methane and ethylene inside the International Space Station to study how diffusion flames behave in microgravity. By removing gravity-driven buoyancy, researchers could better observe flame shapes, temperatures, and soot formation. Understanding these microgravity flames helps improve computational models used for spacecraft fire safety and combustion efficiency.
summary_expert: The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame) investigation utilized the ACME in CIR hardware on the International Space Station to study weak coflow diffusion flames and sooting tendencies using gas fuels including 100% C2H4, 100% CH4, 30% C2H4, 40% CH4, and 50% C2H4. The test matrix varied fuel compositions, resulting in multiple ignition outcomes ranging across different test runs (for example, 16 flames ignited in 6 tests, down to individual runs with fewer ignitions). Variables that changed between tests included the fuel type, while objectives focused on characterizing flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures, extinction limits, soot luminosity, and soot volume fractions as a function of velocity and fuel dilution.

key_findings.text: The fuels and sample materials tested in ACME CLD Flame were 100% C2H4, 100% CH4, 30% C2H4, 40% CH4, and 50% C2H4 gas fuels.

Recorded test outcomes in ACME CLD Flame include 16 flames ignited in 6 tests, 14 flames ignited in 4 tests, 10 flames ignited in 3 tests, 8 flames ignited in 3 tests, 3 flames ignited in 3 tests, 9 flames ignited in 3 tests, 13 flames ignited in 2 tests, 5 flames ignited in 1 tests, 7 flames ignited in 1 tests, 2 flames ignited in 1 tests, 18 flames ignited in 1 tests, 6 flames ignited in 1 tests, 12 flames ignited in 1 tests, 15 flames ignited in 1 tests, and 11 flames ignited in 1 tests.
